explanations.answer: He prays to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, spreads out his hands and speaks straight to God. His words start with "O LORD, God of Israel…" and in verse 28 he calls what he's doing a prayer. Hands up, whole crowd watching, and he talks to God like nobody else is in the room. That's a man who knows who he's talking to.

explanations.answer: He reads from the law
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage has Solomon, Israel's king, reading anything. His hands are spread toward heaven, and he speaks to the LORD directly. He even says "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You…" No scroll in sight, friend. Just a king talking to God.

explanations.answer: He sings a song of David
explanations.explanation: The text says Solomon, Israel's king, "said," and it never mentions a song. He does bring up his father David, but only to talk about God's promise to him. What Solomon is doing is praying to the LORD. I've sung in the shower and called it a concert, but this isn't that.

explanations.answer: Those who walk before Him with all their hearts
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says God keeps His covenant of loving devotion with "Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts." The word is ALL. Not half, not most of the time, not when it's convenient. I once put in about forty percent effort on a batch, and the cookies knew.

explanations.answer: Those who bring Him the most offerings
explanations.explanation: Solomon never ties God's covenant of loving devotion to who brings the most offerings. He says it's kept with servants who walk before God with all their hearts. This is a prayer about the heart, friend, not a scoreboard. Nobody gets a bigger cookie for a bigger pile.

explanations.answer: Those who were born in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Where someone was born doesn't come up in Solomon's words. He says God keeps His covenant of loving devotion with servants "who walk before You with all their hearts." That's about how a person walks with God. Nobody needs a Jerusalem birth certificate for that.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says the opposite. He tells God, "You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David." David was Israel's king before him. Then Solomon adds, "What You spoke with Your mouth You have fulfilled with Your hand this day." So for this promise, the waiting is over.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, because Solomon, Israel's king, says God has already done it. He tells God, "You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David." David was Israel's king before him. Solomon adds that what God spoke with His mouth, He fulfilled with His hand this day. He isn't waiting on that one, friend.

explanations.answer: David would never fail to have a man on it
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. Solomon quotes God telling David, "You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel…" David was Israel's king before Solomon. The promise is about a man always being on that throne, and it has a condition attached, which comes right up.

explanations.answer: It would move to a bigger city
explanations.explanation: God's promise to David, Israel's king before Solomon, isn't about moving the throne anywhere. As Solomon quotes it, God said, "You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel…" So the promise is about someone always sitting on it. Nothing in this passage mentions a bigger city.

explanations.answer: Solomon would sit on it forever
explanations.explanation: Solomon quotes God's promise to his father David, and it doesn't name Solomon at all. God said, "You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel…" And that promise came with an "if only," about David's descendants guarding their way. It's a man on the throne, and the promise doesn't say who.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Solomon quotes the whole thing: "if only your descendants guard their way to walk before Me as you have done." David was Israel's king before him, and the throne promise was spoken to David. So there's an "if only" in the middle of it. Listen for those little words, friend, they carry weight.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: The promise did come with a condition. Solomon quotes God telling David, Israel's king before him, "if only your descendants guard their way to walk before Me as you have done." That "if only" is right there in verse 25. A promise with fine print, and Solomon reads it out loud.

explanations.answer: It can't contain God and neither can heaven
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says it plainly: "The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built." He built the temple himself and still says it. I can't even fit all my cookie cutters in one drawer, and he's talking about God not fitting in heaven. Humbling stuff.

explanations.answer: God will now live only inside it
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks, "But will God indeed dwell upon the earth?" Then he says the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain God, much less this temple. So he's not saying God lives only inside it. He's saying nothing built can hold Him.

explanations.answer: It's grand enough to hold all of God
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says the opposite. "The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built." If the highest heavens can't hold God, a building can't either, however grand it is. He built the thing and he's the first to say so.

explanations.answer: So He'll hear prayers prayed toward it
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to keep His eyes open toward the temple "so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place." It's about God hearing prayers. Open eyes, open ears, night and day. That's a lot of attention, friend.

explanations.answer: So He'll guard it from enemies
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, gives a different reason in verse 29. He asks God's eyes to be open toward the temple "so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place." Guarding the temple from enemies isn't what he says here. The reason he gives is prayer.

explanations.answer: So He'll watch over the priests
explanations.explanation: The priests don't come up in Solomon's request, friend. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to keep His eyes open toward the temple "so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place." The reason is that God would hear prayer.

explanations.answer: heaven
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says, "May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place." Prayers go toward the temple, but he places God's dwelling in heaven. That fits what he just said, that even the highest heavens can't contain God (verse 27).

explanations.answer: Zion
explanations.explanation: Zion doesn't show up in this prayer at all. Solomon, Israel's king, says, "May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place." The people pray toward the temple, but God's dwelling place is heaven. Good guess on a place name, though.

explanations.answer: the temple
explanations.explanation: Close, since the people pray toward the temple. But Solomon, Israel's king, says, "May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place." Just before this, he said the highest heavens can't contain God, much less this temple (verse 27). So the temple is where people turn, and heaven is where he places God's dwelling.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks for both in one breath: "May You hear and forgive." Hear their plea, and then forgive. You'll notice that second part keeps coming back through the whole prayer.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks for both. Verse 30 says, "May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. May You hear and forgive." Hearing and forgiving go together right there, and he keeps asking for forgiveness all through this prayer.

explanations.answer: Condemn the wicked and justify the righteous
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to act and to judge. He asks for "condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done, and justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness." He's asking God to sort it out. No dough gets sorted fairer than that.

explanations.answer: Forgive them both and send them home
explanations.explanation: Not in this situation, friend. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to hear from heaven and act, and to judge. That means "condemning the wicked man" and "justifying the righteous man." Forgiveness shows up in the next situations, but here it's about judging between two men.

explanations.answer: Let the priests settle the whole matter
explanations.explanation: The priests don't come up here. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God Himself to "hear from heaven and act." He asks God to judge, condemning the wicked and justifying the righteous. The one settling it is God, from heaven.

explanations.answer: Returning to God and praying in the temple
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. Solomon, Israel's king, imagines the people defeated because of sin, and then "they return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading with You in this temple." The turn is toward God, not toward a plan B. Nobody ends up lost for long in that direction.

explanations.answer: Gathering a bigger army to fight again
explanations.explanation: That's not the picture Solomon, Israel's king, paints. After the defeat, he says the people "return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading with You in this temple." Their next move is back to God. The army isn't the first thing on his mind.

explanations.answer: Leaving the land to start over somewhere
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, pictures the opposite. The people return to God and pray in the temple, and then he asks God to restore them to the land (verse 34). They're not packing up. They're coming back to God, and he asks God to bring them back to the land.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks for something different. He prays, "May You restore them to the land You gave to their fathers." It's the same land, handed back, not a brand new one. He asks forgiveness first, and the land follows.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right. Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't ask for a new land. He asks God to "forgive the sin of Your people Israel" and to "restore them to the land You gave to their fathers." The same land, given back.

explanations.answer: confess
explanations.explanation: Verse 35 says the people "pray toward this place and confess Your name." Solomon, Israel's king, pictures them confessing God's name when the rain is gone. They look to God, and that's the first blank filled.

explanations.answer: turn
explanations.explanation: The second blank is "turn." Solomon, Israel's king, says the people "turn from their sins because You have afflicted them." They confess God's name, and they turn from their sins.

explanations.answer: forget
explanations.explanation: Forgetting is the opposite of what Solomon, Israel's king, pictures. The people "confess Your name," which means they bring God's name to mind and say it out loud. Forgetting would have them walking away from it. I once forgot cookies in the oven, and that's the kind of forgetting that makes a mess.

explanations.answer: hide
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't in Solomon's picture. Solomon, Israel's king, says the people "pray toward this place and confess Your name, and they turn from their sins." They come toward God instead of hiding from Him. The temple is where they turn their hands.

explanations.answer: curse
explanations.explanation: Cursing isn't what the people do in Solomon's prayer. He pictures them praying and confessing God's name and turning from their sins. Solomon is Israel's king, and he's asking for forgiveness here. A cursing crowd would be a very different prayer, friend.

explanations.answer: Teach them the good way to walk
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to forgive "so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk." Then he asks for rain too. So there's a teacher in this prayer, and it's God.

explanations.answer: Give them a brand new law
explanations.explanation: A new law isn't what Solomon, Israel's king, asks for. He asks God to forgive and send rain, "so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk." He wants God to teach the way, and a new rulebook isn't in the request.

explanations.answer: Make them the richest nation
explanations.explanation: Riches aren't on Solomon's list here. Solomon, Israel's king, asks for forgiveness and rain, and that God would "teach them the good way in which they should walk." The rain is on the land God gave as an inheritance. Being the richest isn't part of this ask.

explanations.answer: According to all his ways
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart." And he adds that God alone knows the hearts of all men. Only someone who sees the heart can judge fairly. That's not a job for a stamper.

explanations.answer: According to what the priests decide
explanations.explanation: The priests don't decide anything in this part of Solomon's prayer. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart." The one doing the repaying is God, who knows the heart.

explanations.answer: According to the size of his offering
explanations.explanation: Offerings don't come up here. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart." It's about the man's ways and his heart. The size of a gift doesn't come into it.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says it right there: "for You alone know the hearts of all men." That's why he asks God to repay each man according to his ways, since God knows his heart. No one else can see all the way in.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. Solomon, Israel's king, prays, "for You alone know the hearts of all men." Alone means alone, friend. That's why the judging is left to God.

explanations.answer: Do all the foreigner asks Him
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You." That's a wide open door. Someone from a distant land who prays toward the temple gets God's ear too.

explanations.answer: Send him back to his own land
explanations.explanation: Sending him away isn't what Solomon, Israel's king, asks. He asks God to "hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You." The foreigner has come because of God's name, and Solomon wants his prayer answered.

explanations.answer: Have him go through a priest
explanations.explanation: No priest is mentioned for the foreigner. Solomon, Israel's king, pictures him coming and praying toward the temple. Then he asks God to "hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You." The foreigner's prayer goes straight to God.

explanations.answer: All peoples will know God's name
explanations.explanation: That's what Solomon, Israel's king, says: "Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel." One foreigner's answered prayer, and the word spreads. He also says they will know this house is called by God's Name.

explanations.answer: The foreigner will move to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Moving isn't part of what Solomon, Israel's king, says. He says that if God answers, "all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You." The result is that people everywhere know God's name.

explanations.answer: Israel will grow richer and stronger
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't name wealth or strength as the result. He says, "Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel." The result he pictures is that the whole earth knows God's name.

explanations.answer: Hear them and uphold their cause
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks, "then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause." The people are out at war, praying toward the city God chose. He asks for God's ear and God's backing.

explanations.answer: Bring them home before the fight
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, pictures them going to war "wherever You send them," so he isn't asking for them to be called back first. He asks God to "hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause." The request is for God to hear and uphold.

explanations.answer: Keep the temple safe while they're gone
explanations.explanation: The temple's safety isn't part of this request. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause." The prayer is for the people at war.

explanations.answer: An enemy takes them captive to his land
explanations.explanation: That's what Solomon, Israel's king, pictures. He says God becomes angry and delivers them "to an enemy who takes them as captives to his own land, whether far or near." It's a heavy part of the prayer. And he follows it right away with a way back.

explanations.answer: The temple falls down to the ground
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't picture the temple falling here. He pictures God delivering the people "to an enemy who takes them as captives to his own land, whether far or near." It's the people who are taken. This is a heavy moment in the prayer.

explanations.answer: Their king is driven from the throne
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't mention a king being driven off in this verse. What he says is that God delivers the people "to an enemy who takes them as captives to his own land, whether far or near." The picture is captivity for the people. It's a heavy part of the prayer.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, pictures that very thing. In verse 47 they "come to their senses in the land to which they were taken, and they repent and plead with You in the land of their captors." They say they have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly. Honest words, in a hard place.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, does picture it. He says they "come to their senses in the land to which they were taken, and they repent." They admit they have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly. A captive land isn't too far for that prayer.

explanations.answer: With all their heart and soul
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says they "return to You with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them captive." All their heart and soul, even there. That's a full return, with nothing held back.

explanations.answer: With gifts for the temple
explanations.explanation: Gifts aren't how Solomon, Israel's king, pictures the return. He says they "return to You with all their heart and soul." They come back with themselves, heart and soul.

explanations.answer: With a new king to lead them
explanations.explanation: A new king isn't part of the picture. Solomon, Israel's king, says they "return to You with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them captive." It's their heart and soul that go back to God.

explanations.answer: compassion
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors to show them mercy." He's asking God to soften the hearts of the people holding them. That's a prayer for mercy where it looks least likely.

explanations.answer: strength
explanations.explanation: Strength isn't what Solomon, Israel's king, asks for here. He asks God to "grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors to show them mercy." The word is compassion, and it's aimed at the captors' eyes.

explanations.answer: riches
explanations.explanation: Riches aren't the ask. Solomon, Israel's king, prays that God would "grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors to show them mercy." Compassion is what he asks for, friend. The captives need mercy, not money.

explanations.answer: They're His people and His inheritance
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Solomon, Israel's king, gives: "For they are Your people and Your inheritance." He reminds God of who they belong to. Then he adds that God brought them out of Egypt.

explanations.answer: They built Him a beautiful temple
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't use the temple as his reason. He says, "For they are Your people and Your inheritance; You brought them out of Egypt, out of the furnace for iron." The reason is who they are to God.

explanations.answer: They've suffered long enough already
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't say that. His reason is, "For they are Your people and Your inheritance." He points to who they belong to, and to God bringing them out of Egypt.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Solomon, Israel's king, asks God to "listen to them whenever they call to You." Whenever, friend. He even pictures captives praying "in the direction of" the land, the city and the house (verse 48), far from the temple itself.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right. Solomon, Israel's king, prays, "May Your eyes be open to the pleas of Your servant and of Your people Israel, and may You listen to them whenever they call to You." That's whenever, not only inside one building. He even pictures captives praying toward the city and the house from an enemy's land.

explanations.answer: Moses
explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says God set Israel apart "as You spoke through Your servant Moses when You brought our fathers out of Egypt." Moses was Israel's leader. The prayer ends by pointing back to that old word.

explanations.answer: Samuel
explanations.explanation: Samuel, the prophet who anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13), isn't the name Solomon gives here. Solomon, Israel's king, says God spoke "through Your servant Moses when You brought our fathers out of Egypt." So the name is Moses, Israel's leader.

explanations.answer: David
explanations.explanation: David, Solomon's father, comes up earlier in the prayer, but not here. Solomon, Israel's king, says God spoke "through Your servant Moses when You brought our fathers out of Egypt." So the name is Moses, Israel's leader.
